what_it_does: A key safety technique for critical systems is to run the same computation twice on different hardware and check that both answers match — if they disagree, something went wrong. Modern high-performance processors (called out-of-order superscalar cores) execute instructions in a complicated, reordered way that makes it very difficult to attach a second 'shadow' processor for this kind of redundancy check without heavily redesigning the chip. MEEK proposes a cleaner split of responsibilities: the fast, complex main core runs the program normally, while one or more simpler, lower-power helper cores re-run the same instructions and compare results. Instead of wiring everything together in hardware, the design uses a small amount of software coordination and minor adjustments to the operating system to synchronize the main and helper cores, catching errors within microseconds. The approach deliberately avoids deep changes to the main processor's internal design, making it more practical to adopt in real products.
